'''''Clinopodium nepeta''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]]: ''Calamintha nepeta''), known as '''lesser calamint''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a perennial herb of the [[mint family]] known for having fragrant, grey-green, oregano-like leaves with a [[Mentha pulegium|pennyroyal]]  smell. It is also called niepita, and mentuccia romana. This plant commonly grows across the Mediterranean, North Africa and parts of Central Asia and has traditionally been used as a folk medicine and culinary herb.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vlachou |first1=Georgia |last2=Papafotiou |first2=Maria |last3=Bertsouklis |first3=Konstantinos F. |title=Studies on Seed Germination and Micropropagation of Clinopodium nepeta: A Medicinal and Aromatic Plant |journal=HortScience |date=September 2019 |volume=54 |issue=9 |pages=1558–1564 |doi=10.21273/HORTSCI13996-19|doi-access=free }}</ref> A recent study also found cultivars of lesser catmint that had the same compounds in [[catnip]] that cause the euphoric effect in [[cats]], known as [[nepetalactone]].<ref name= "Chemical Variability in Clinopodium nepeta">{{cite journal |last1=Zorde |first1=Martin |last2=Lockhart |first2=Anthony |last3=Vasilatis |first3=Ariane |last4=Gomes |first4=Erik |last5=Wu |first5=Qingli |last6=Simon |first6=James |title=Chemical Variability in Clinopodium nepeta: A New Source of Nepetalactones |journal=Journal of Medicinally Active Plants |date=28 March 2024 |volume=13 |issue=1 |doi=10.7275/jmap.2034}}</ref> 

==Description==
[[File:Calamintha nepeta Sturm54.jpg|thumb|left|[[Botanical illustration]] of ''Clinopodium nepeta'' (titled as ''Thymus nepeta'') from [[Deutschlands Flora in Abbildungen]] (1796)]]
Lesser calamint is a perennial shrub, forming a compact mound of shiny green [[oregano]]-like leaves. The flowers are lavender pink. The plant reaches a  height of {{convert|18|in|cm|order=flip|abbr=off}}.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.crimson-sage.com/shop/?cart=517047&cat=1&itemid=100157& | title=Organic Medicinal Herb Plants for Sale | access-date=2009-09-09 | archive-date=2011-07-08 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708203956/http://www.crimson-sage.com/shop/?cart=517047&cat=1&itemid=100157& | url-status=live }}</ref> The lesser calamint smells like a cross between mint and oregano. It attracts honeybees and butterflies.<ref name="FineGardening">{{Cite web | url=http://www.finegardening.com/plantguide/calamintha-nepeta-nepetoides-lesser-calamint.aspx | title=Lesser calamint | access-date=2009-09-09 | archive-date=2009-11-03 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103190551/http://www.finegardening.com/plantguide/calamintha-nepeta-nepetoides-lesser-calamint.aspx | url-status=live }}</ref> Lesser calamint usually grows in the summer and well into the fall. It can become dormant in the winter months then reblossom in spring. In fall the flowers fall to the ground and will self-seed. Seedlings will flower in late August.<ref name="FineGardening" /> Lesser calamint often grows wild but can also be kept in pots. The average [[life expectancy]] of a plant is 3–4 years. It is susceptible to [[powdery mildew]].<ref name="FineGardening" />

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 as ''Melissa nepeta''. It was subsequently placed in ''[[Calamintha]]'', ''[[Thymus (plant)|Thymus]]'', ''[[Satureja]]'' and ''[[Clinopodium]]'', among other genera. The last of these is currently accepted by the [[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]].<ref name=WCSP_43618 />

===Subspecies===
Three subspecies are recognized:<ref name=WCSP_43618 />
* [[Clinopodium nepeta subsp. nepeta|''Clinopodium nepeta'' subsp. ''nepeta'']] – South Central and Southern Europe to Northern Iran
* ''Clinopodium nepeta'' subsp. ''spruneri'' – Mediterranean to the Caucasus
* ''Clinopodium nepeta'' subsp. ''subisodontum'' – East Central and Southeast Europe

==Uses==
Lesser calamint is commonly used as a herb in the  [[Italian cuisine|Italian]] and [[Cuisine of Corsica|Corsican cuisine]], where it is called ''nepita'', ''mentuccia'', ''nipitella'' or ''nepitella''. In Rome it is used in the preparation of the [[Carciofi alla Romana]]. In southern Italy it is used in the making of a goat cheese called ''cassiedu'', giving the cheese a minty taste.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |author-link=Andrea Pieroni (ethnobotanist) |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=39 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref> Some sources state that ''[[Nepeta nepetella]]'' can be used in cooking like the lesser calamint.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mentuccia, nepetella o nepitella? Facciamo un po' di chiarezza |url=https://www.valfrutta.it/magazine/mentuccia-nepetella-o-nepitella-facciamo-un-po-di-chiarezza/ |website=Valfrutta |access-date=14 May 2020 |language=it |archive-date=20 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920015053/https://www.valfrutta.it/magazine/mentuccia-nepetella-o-nepitella-facciamo-un-po-di-chiarezza/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

''C. nepeta'' has a long history of use as a herbal medicine as a tea for cramps and the digestive tract.<ref name= "Clinopodium nepeta (L.) Kuntze from Bosnia and Herzegovina Chemical Characterisation of Headspace and Essential Oil of Fresh and Dried Samples">{{cite journal |last1=Džudžević-Čančar |first1=Hurija |last2=Boškailo |first2=Emina |last3=Dedić |first3=Alema |last4=Marijanović |first4=Zvonimir |last5=Alispahić |first5=Amra |last6=Čančar |first6=Ismet Fatih |last7=Vidic |first7=Danijela |last8=Jerković |first8=Igor |title=Clinopodium nepeta (L.) Kuntze from Bosnia and Herzegovina: Chemical Characterisation of Headspace and Essential Oil of Fresh and Dried Samples |journal=Records of Natural Products |date=1 January 2023 |issue=2 |pages=300–311 |doi=10.25135/rnp.357.2207.2504|doi-access=free }}</ref> Additionally [[Steam distillation|hydrodistilled]] essential oil made from ''C. nepeta'' has been used to alleviate insomnia, headache and respiratory illness<ref name= "Clinopodium nepeta (L.) Kuntze from Bosnia and Herzegovina Chemical Characterisation of Headspace and Essential Oil of Fresh and Dried Samples"/>

Research has found that extracts of ''C. nepeta'', such as essential oils, have antifungal, insecticidal and insect-repellent properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Debbabi |first1=Haïfa |last2=El Mokni |first2=Ridha |last3=Chaieb |first3=Ikbal |last4=Nardoni |first4=Simona |last5=Maggi |first5=Filippo |last6=Caprioli |first6=Giovanni |last7=Hammami |first7=Saoussen |title=Chemical Composition, Antifungal and Insecticidal Activities of the Essential Oils from Tunisian Clinopodium nepeta subsp. nepeta and Clinopodium nepeta subsp. glandulosum |journal=Molecules |date=2 May 2020 |volume=25 |issue=9 |pages=2137 |doi=10.3390/molecules25092137|doi-access=free |pmid=32370305 |pmc=7249092 }}</ref> Moreover it has recently been discovered that some cultivars of ''C. nepeta'' contain [[nepetalactone]], the compound in true [[catnip]] famous for the euphoric effect it has on cats.  This may also contribute to insect-repellent properties of extracts made from ''C. nepeta'' plants.<ref name= "Chemical Variability in Clinopodium nepeta"/>
